headline: Moriches Inlet's Ebb Cut Is Doing the Sorting Work For You
subhead: Building tidal flow off the new moon has bass and blues stacking on the same current seams that fluke and porgies are using to feed — read the cut right and you can hit three species off one drift.
body_markdown:
I spent an hour at the west jetty Tuesday just watching the water move before I made a cast, and what I saw told me more than any gauge could. The ebb was running hard off that new moon — two days past now — and the sand shoal off the west side is pushing the outflow into a tighter, faster lane than I've seen most of the summer. That's the storm-cut geometry doing what it does after a strong tidal cycle: the channel scours a little deeper, the current accelerates through the throat, and everything that swims gets funneled into a lane about sixty yards wide instead of spreading across the whole inlet mouth. Bait has no choice but to ride it. Predators know that.

We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon should sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's showing up now. The bass aren't blitzing on the surface like they are up in the Sound and further east, but they're stacked tight along that ebb seam on the drop, holding just off the bottom where the current breaks over the shoal edge. I've been running a 1.5-ounce bucktail, white or chartreuse, letting it sink all the way to the bottom on the upcurrent side and then working it back with the tide instead of against it — that's the mistake I see guys make here, fighting the flow instead of using it. Slot fish in the 28-32 inch range have been coming off that drift on the last two hours of the outgoing, with the occasional overslot mixed in for guys soaking bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig anchored just inside the jetty rocks.

Bluefish are the more reliable story right now. They're working both tide changes at the inlet, slashing through peanut bunker that's been pushed out of the bay on the ebb and pinned against the jetty rocks. Diamond jigs — half-ounce to one-ounce depending on how much current you're fighting — worked with a fast, erratic retrieve have been drawing steady strikes, and if you want to save your fingers, a wire leader in front of anything metal is not optional right now. These aren't the biggest blues of the year but they're consistent, and consistent is worth something when the ocean's been ugly.

Speaking of ugly — the open beach at Cupsogue has been a tough go this week. Swell's been running close to four feet with a short five-second period, which means it's steep, sloppy, and hard to read from the sand. That kind of wave energy churns the surf zone and pushes bait and predators off the outer bar into calmer, current-protected water. That's exactly why the inlet structure itself — the jetty rocks, the edges of the main channel, the flats behind Tuthill Point — has been outproducing the open beach. If you're set on surf fishing Cupsogue, I'd wait for a lull between swell trains or fish the last two hours of light when the wind typically backs off, but don't expect the classic sandbar bite you get on calmer weeks. The energy just isn't letting fish sit up on that bar right now.

Fluke fishing inside the bay is fair, not great — which is honestly about right for mid-August. The channel edges off Pattersquash and the deeper cuts near the Route 51 bridge are holding fish, but you're working through a lot of shorts to find a keeper. Five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the drop-offs where the channel meets the flat, have been the most efficient way to sort through the population without burning through bait. If you want a shot at a bigger fish, work the deeper holes on the last of the incoming when bait gets pushed up onto the flats and fluke slide up to ambush it.

Bottom fishing has been the quiet bright spot. Sea bass and porgies on the inlet structure and the nearby rock piles are settling into that reliable late-summer pattern — small hooks, fresh clam or squid strips, and enough weight to hold bottom in the current has been putting a mixed bag in the cooler for anyone willing to grind through the short fish. It's not glamorous, but it's the most dependable meal you'll bring home off this stretch of water right now.

Weakfish have been quiet — I haven't heard of a legitimate weakfish report out of the bay in weeks, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If you're targeting them, you're burning time better spent on bass or blues.

Looking ahead, I expect that ebb-seam pattern at the inlet to hold or even sharpen over the next several days as the tidal range keeps building toward the next set of strong currents. If the swell backs off even a foot, I'd get back out to Cupsogue and work the bar on an early outgoing — that's when bait gets flushed out of the bay and stripers historically set up on the outer edge to intercept it. Inside the bay, I'd keep working those channel edges on fluke through the week, but don't expect the ratio of keepers to shorts to improve much until water temperatures ease off later in the month. And with bunker-driven bass activity blowing up everywhere from the Sound down through southern New England, I wouldn't be shocked if we start seeing more visible surface activity here too once that bait pushes further down the coast — worth keeping an eye on the inlet mouth at first light.
